paras: The attacks on Black Western Union messengers in Richmond took place on December 2, 1903, when white boys described as strikers or strike sympathizers stabbed a Black messenger, James Randolph, in the shoulder and drove a second Black messenger from his bicycle with bricks during a strike of white messenger boys against a pay cut and the hiring of Black replacements. No arrests for either attack were reported, and the Richmond Times-Dispatch wrote that public sentiment was 'largely with the boys.' The story ran widely, while the Richmond Planet, a Black weekly, later wrote that the new messengers had met 'brutal treatment' without quailing.

The white messenger boys of the Western Union Telegraph Company in Richmond went on strike on December 1, 1903, over a cut in pay, and the company began filling their places with Black workers. A Times-Dispatch editorial put the new rate at a cent and a half per delivery or call, down from two cents or more, while the wire reports called it a 25 per cent reduction. The same editorial granted the company's legal right to hire Black replacements but held that 'the people of this community prefer white messengers to negro messengers' and predicted the experiment would prove costly.

On December 2 the Times-Dispatch counted several attacks on the Black replacements. Randolph was 'set upon by a gang of white boys' and received a stab wound in the shoulder about an inch long, which the paper called severe but 'not at all serio[us]', adding that the assailant was not identified; the wire said he was stabbed with a pocket knife in the evening by 'strikers or strike sympathizers.'

That afternoon, near the corner of Governor and Franklin streets, a 'gang of small boys' surrounded a second, unnamed Black messenger and pelted him with bricks and stones until he abandoned his bicycle. One of the boys then jumped on the wheel and smashed its spokes, or, in the wire's words, the bicycle was 'stamped on and broken to pieces.' In a third incident the same day, police arrested a striking messenger boy suspected of hitting a Black messenger with a rock, but released him because he could not be identified as the thrower.

No arrest for the stabbing or the bicycle attack appears in the coverage, and the boys in the bicycle attack 'escaped detection.' The Times-Dispatch said the Black messengers had to look carefully to avoid missiles and that police were trying to prevent violence, but added that 'the boys are too sharp to be caught in violence.' The company reported twenty-four Black messengers on duty and deliveries about as usual.
The Black messengers kept their jobs: by January 1904 the Richmond Planet reported that they were 'giving satisfaction,' were being issued uniforms, and that the feeling against them was subsiding.

The Richmond dispatch dated December 2 appeared the next day in the Savannah Morning News, the Alexandria Gazette and the Birmingham Age-Herald. Over the following days it ran in the Raleigh News & Observer, the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger and the Fredericksburg Free Lance, which closed with the line 'Public sympathy is largely with the striking messengers.' Headlines differed in whom they put first: Savannah's read 'Western Union Boys Violent at Richmond' and Birmingham's 'Messenger Boys at Richmond Assault Their Negro Substitutes,' while Raleigh's was 'Negro Messengers Attacked.'
The Times-Dispatch, the city's own paper, gave the fullest account under the headline 'The Negroes Still Carry Telegrams,' setting the attacks beside the strikers' grievances.

No Black paper in the coverage named Randolph or described the stabbing. The Richmond Planet instead wrote on December 12 that the Black replacements had been 'subjected to brutal treatment at first, but not one has quailed in the face of duty.' A week later the Planet denounced the Richmond News-Leader for urging white business men to boycott Western Union, calling the appeal 'one of the most remarkable appeals to race prejudice' it had seen and an unlawful boycott. The St. Paul Appeal noted only that white Richmonders 'became very indignant and boycotted the line.' Where the white papers framed the violence as an outgrowth of a strike that had public sympathy, the Planet framed it as a test that Black workers had passed.

reader.title: Attacks on Black Western Union messengers in Richmond, 1903
bases: Gangs of white boys described as strikers or strike sympathizers stabbed one Black replacement messenger and stoned another off his bicycle during a messenger strike (A3, A5); the violence was by a crowd against individuals, in a labor setting.
The Richmond Times-Dispatch's own report (A3) and the independent Richmond wire dispatch (A4, A5, A7) agree on the stabbing of James Randolph and the bricking of a second messenger on December 2.

accounts.label: Richmond Times-Dispatch (local report)
accounts.gist: Randolph was set upon by a gang of white boys and stabbed, the assailant unidentified; a second messenger was bricked off his wheel by small boys who escaped; a boy arrested over a rock was discharged.

accounts.label: Richmond wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Strikers or strike sympathizers stabbed Randolph with a pocket knife in the evening and a party of boys broke another messenger's bicycle; no arrests made.

accounts.label: Company representative
accounts.gist: The company had 24 colored messengers delivering as usual and said negro men should carry messages because the work demoralized boys.

accounts.label: Black editorial (Richmond Planet)
accounts.gist: The colored replacements met brutal treatment at first but none quailed, and they rendered most satisfactory service.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'The Negroes Still Carry Telegrams' and reported the attacks, but said public sentiment was 'largely with the boys' and that 'the boys are too sharp to be caught in violence'; its editorial a day earlier said the community preferred white messengers.

Wire reprints under 'Western Union Boys Violent at Richmond', 'Messenger Boys at Richmond Assault Their Negro Substitutes', 'Negro Messengers Attacked' and 'Strikers Attack Negroes', several adding that public sympathy was with the strikers.
The Richmond Planet called the treatment of the messengers 'brutal' and praised their steadiness, and later attacked the News-Leader's boycott call as an appeal to race prejudice.
The St. Paul Appeal noted only the strike, the Black replacements and the white boycott of the line.
